title: Nothing Left to Tell
passages:
Miko read the curl a second time, slower, so there was no mistaking the digits. Four-two-one-seven. She said it out loud, loud enough to travel across the dirt to where Dray sat on his running board.

Dray went still. His work lamp stayed off. His hand rested on the crank in his pocket but didn’t close around it. The book stayed inside his coat, unopened.

“That’s Rig Seven,” he said. “Plate 4217. Dark eleven months. Supposed to be asleep in my shed with the other ten.”

He knew it on sight. Miko saw it in the way his jaw tightened, in the way his eyes stayed fixed on the reader’s curl like it had just named a man he thought was dead.

“Somebody’s been running Culvert Nine’s cans to it,” she said. “Eleven cans logged against that plate. Receiving mark C9. That’s our whole count, Dray. That’s Brill’s winter on a line that’s supposed to be dark.”

Dray didn’t answer right away. He let the number sit between them, lamplight from his rig throwing his shadow long and thin behind him.

He wouldn’t cross the door plate. He’d said he’d wait as long as his fuel held—three weeks, if it came to that—and he meant it. Forty meters short of Culvert Nine’s steel, lamp on the ground, no schedule, no rush. But the rule was the rule, and he held to it to the letter. A rig lived only while a living name was wired to its crew plate. A blank rig was a parts pile. He wouldn’t crack the book for anyone, not even to check whether one of his own sleepers had been stolen and fed.

“The rule stands,” Dray said. “A living name on my steel, two witnesses, then every page opens. Until then, 4217 stays dark in my book and dark in my yard.”

He let that sit there, too. The same hand that had cut Kass’s line at 04:51—the rescinded Anza clearance struck through the blank rig’s ground-off plate, the same minute a ghost rig had vanished from Kettering’s master board—was feeding one of his own rigs Culvert Nine’s cans. Someone knew his book. Someone knew which plate was supposed to be dark. Someone had run eleven cans against it, and the reader had logged them good.

Brill stood in the jaw’s shadow, arms crossed, saying nothing. She trusted her storeroom over any person’s word, and right now her storeroom was eleven cans lighter than it should have been. Saul stood near the door plate with their come-along quiet in their hands, the steel cable slack. Kass had Nour’s tally card stuffed in their shirt, their bad knee braced against the grade, waiting.

Dray didn’t look at any of them. He looked at the reader’s curl, then back at Miko.

His forty riders were wired to their plates in Marrow Cut. If one of his plates was running south with Culvert Nine’s seal, those riders weren’t just part of the yard anymore. They were part of the count. They were part of the debt.

Miko stepped to the edge of Dray's lamplight. The dirt was cold through her boots, but she kept her voice level. "You want a name," she said. "I got one."

Dray didn't move. His hand stayed on the crank in his pocket. "Go on."

"J. Renner," Miko said. "Loader. Anza overlap log—the shift-handover record that says who's on and who's off. That means live, that means on the books, that means not sealed inside a pod somewhere." She tapped her own coat where badge C9-047 sat under her collar, the bit of tin that let a station loader open a receiving jaw. "I put Renner on your crew plate, wired to Rig Seven, and you cut the rig loose with eleven cans. That's your price. I take a cut, I ride out before winter, and Culvert Nine gets its count back."

Brill didn't speak. Saul didn't speak. Kass stayed braced against the grade with Nour's tally card stuffed in their shirt, watching Miko like she was a rig about to throw a bearing.

Dray looked at the reader's curl, then at Miko. "You're selling me a name to save your own hide."

"I'm selling you a living name," Miko said. "That's what your book runs on. Renner's name is live on Anza's overlap log. I saw it this morning."

Dray shook his head. "I take a name at its word. I don't take a stranger's word that the name is still breathing." He turned toward the crew box behind the seat. "Reader two at Anza. I wire Renner into it, ask if the name's live and free to put on a plate. If it comes back clean, every page opens. If it comes back dead, you're chalk dust."

"That's fair," Miko said.

"Nothing about this is fair," Dray said. He looked at Saul and Brill, then at Kass. "Two witnesses. Pick yourselves."

Saul's come-along hung slack in their hands. Brill's arms were still crossed, her face unreadable in the lamplight. Kass had shifted their weight onto their good leg, Nour's card pressed against their ribs.

Miko looked at Dray. "J. Renner," she said, loud enough for the wire to carry. "Loader. Anza overlap log. Live and free."

Dray held her gaze for a long moment, then nodded once. He turned back to the dark opening of the crew box and reached inside for the reader.

Dray pulled the reader from the crew box. It was a heavy handset with brass knobs and a wire that ran back to the rig’s battery. He snapped the lead onto the terminal plate and spoke J. Renner into the mouthpiece.

The wire crackled. Then Teodoro’s voice came out of the speaker, thick with shop grease and the wet rasp of Ivo’s respirator behind him.

“Reader two,” Teodoro said. “Anza relay terminal. You’re asking about a name on a plate.”

“J. Renner,” Dray said. “Loader. Anza overlap log. Is the name live? Free to wire to a crew plate?”

“I can answer that,” Teodoro said. “And I can answer everything else too, because you asked what you asked and I answer it before I wonder why you’re asking.” There was a clatter, a drawer sliding shut. “J. Renner cleared north on the green coast train three weeks ago. Chalked off the overlap log. Gone. There is no living hand at Anza carrying that name anymore. Miko Keres signed the resupply board under her real name, but she isn’t Renner. Wren Cardoso is listed as shop hand, countersigned by Marlowe, badge 2244. That is what is on Anza’s board right now.”

Dray didn’t move the reader from his mouth. “You don’t ask who’s calling?”

“No,” Teodoro said. “If you wanted me to know, you would have said. The wire carries your question. It doesn’t owe me your reason.”

Behind him, Ivo’s respirator gave one wet, steady huff. Teodoro’s voice went quieter. “Ivo is breathing on mains compressor power. His cartridge is spent. He is still here. Renner is not.”

Dray looked at Miko. She stood at the edge of the lamplight, her hands loose at her sides, her face still level. She had staked her cut on a name that was not breathing.

“Dead,” Dray said.

“Chalked off,” Teodoro said. “Same thing on a crew plate. No living hand to wire it, so the page stays closed. Every page opens only with a living name and two witnesses. You don’t have the first one.”

Miko’s mouth opened, then closed. She looked at Dray’s rig, at the reader still hot in his hand, at the empty wire running back to Anza.

“You didn’t ask who was on the other end,” Dray said.

“I told you,” Teodoro said. “The question is enough.”

The line went quiet except for Ivo’s respirator. Miko’s name was empty. Her cut was dust. And the man at Anza had given away everything he knew without ever asking who wanted it.

Dray didn’t argue. He turned the reader over in his hands, once, twice, and set it back in the crew box.

"Dead’s dead," he said. "A name with no body behind it can’t hold a plate. That’s the letter."

Miko’s mouth opened, then closed. "You said live and free. Renner’s on the overlap log. That’s live."

"He’s chalked off," Dray said. "Teodoro said it. Gone north, no living hand. You sold me a ghost, Miko. Ghosts don’t run rigs."

"I sold you what was written down," she said. Her voice stayed level, but her knuckles were white at her sides. "That’s how your book works, isn’t it? Words on steel."

"Words on steel with a living name wired to them," Dray said. "You’re not wired. Renner’s not wired. So no cut."

He reached into his coat. Not for the book. For a piece of chalk, nubbed and gray. He walked to Culvert Nine’s door plate and made a mark beside Miko Keres—a single line through it, hard enough to chip the chalk.

"Chalked off," Dray said. "You’re not on Culvert Nine’s tally. You’re not on my plate. You’re nowhere."

Then he lifted his hand from his coat pocket and reached out, taking badge C9-047 from Miko’s collar where it sat under her coat. He held it between his fingers, then closed his fist around it.

"No badge," he said. "A chalked name doesn’t get to carry authority. Saul, put it on your board with the rest of the dead."

Saul didn’t move at first. The come-along hung slack in their hands. Then they stepped forward, took the badge from Dray’s fingers, and clipped it to the manifest sheet where Brill’s board lived. The steel cable clinked against the door plate.

Brill said nothing. She stood in the jaw’s shadow, arms crossed, watching.

"Nobody," Dray said, as if he were confirming a manifest line. "You’re nobody on the line, Miko Keres. No plate, no badge, no name with a body behind it."

Miko opened her mouth to say something sharp, something that would bite back, but the lamplight had gone thin and cold, and she had nothing left to put on steel.

Behind them, the blank rig sat in Culvert Nine’s jaw, eleven canisters locked inside, its hand lamp burning in the crew box. Dray’s rig idled forty meters short of the door plate, fuel and patience enough to wait. And Miko stood with forty riders watching her from Marrow Cut.

Dray tucked the book back into his coat. "The rule stands," he said. "Until a living name hits my steel, nothing in this yard moves."

Brill didn't move to stop him. Her arms stayed crossed while Dray closed his fist around the badge and Saul stepped forward to take it. Only when the steel clip bit into the manifest sheet did Brill uncross her arms. She reached into her coat and pulled out a rag—oil-stained, stiff at the edges, the kind she used to wipe seal residue from the jaw's teeth.

She walked to the storeroom board bolted beside the door plate. C9 was cut into the steel there, deep and straight, with eleven notches struck full beside it, matching Nour's card. Miko's name was written in ink below the notches, the ink still dark.

Brill pressed the rag to the name and rubbed. The ink had soaked into the grain; it didn't want to come. She rubbed harder, her shoulder working, until the letters blurred, then faded, then left nothing but a darker smudge on the board.

"A name in pencil won't hold a wire," Saul said. They still held the slack come-along cable, the steel coil quiet in their hands. "And this one won't even hold ink."

Brill didn't look at them. She wiped the rag once more over the blank spot, folded it, and tucked it back in her coat. "A storeroom feeds names on steel," she said. "Not chalk. Not memory. Not a loader who can't open her own jaw." She looked at Miko, her eyes flat. "You're not on it. So there's nothing for you."

Miko's mouth opened. She had a sharp thing ready—something about skimming, about eleven cans locked in a blank rig behind them, about whose winter was really being fed. "You'll eat every can yourself?" she asked. "Eleven cans, Brill. You'll eat them alone?"

Brill's mouth didn't move. "I'll feed my crew," she said. "My crew is on the board. You rubbed yourself off it."

"Then let me ride out with the rig," Miko said. "I don't need your storeroom. I need a seat."

"No seat," Dray said. He hadn't raised his voice. "No plate. No name."

Behind them, the blank rig sat in Culvert Nine's jaw, its hand lamp burning in the crew box, eleven canisters locked inside with the spoiled one sweating on the clamp pin. The spool of wire from Dray's reader still ran back toward Anza, silent now. Teodoro had given everything away, and Miko had nothing left to trade.

Kass pushed off the grade and limped one step closer, tapping the blank smudge on the board with a calloused finger. "You wiped the name," Kass said to Brill, "but the tally still says eleven short. Your crew is eating those cans whether you wipe Miko off the steel or not."

Dray didn't look at Kass. He looked at the rig in the jaw, at the hand lamp burning inside it.

Brill turned her back. She put her hand on the jaw's wheel, the steel teeth that would lock or release the canisters, and didn't turn it. "Nothing in this yard feeds a name that isn't on it," she said. "Not your badge. Not your name."

Miko stood at the edge of the lamplight, her coat collar empty where the badge had been, and watched Brill's hand close on the wheel. There was nothing left at Culvert Nine that would feed her now.
